n: Psalms 113–118 are the ‘Egyptian Hallel,’ sung at Passover. Jesus and his disciples likely sang part of it after the Last Supper. It opens by calling God’s servants to praise his name.

f.g: Hallelujah — this begins the Hallel (‘praise’) psalms.

n: May God’s name be praised now and forever — praise without end in time.

f.w: from this time forth and for evermore

n: From sunrise to sunset — from east to west — praise without limit in space.

f.w: From the rising of the sun

n: The Lord is exalted above every nation, and his glory is above the heavens.
Who compares to the Lord, who sits enthroned on high?

f.w: Who is like unto the LORD

n: Yet this exalted God stoops down to look at heaven and earth. God’s greatness includes his willingness to come near.
He lifts the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap or garbage dump, where outcasts sat. Hannah’s song uses these words.

f.g: An ash heap or refuse pile outside a town.

n: He seats them among princes — a total reversal of fortune.
He gives the childless woman a home and the joy of children — as he did for Sarah, Rachel, and Hannah. In that culture, barrenness brought deep sorrow and shame.
